name: Vibro-Slim

lead:
Vibro-Slim is described as a 1928 vibration weight-loss device. This entry describes the category the product belongs to, the vibrating belt machine.
These machines used a motor-driven belt around the waist to shake the body, and were marketed as a passive way to slim.

paras: In the category, the user stands on a platform beside a post with an electric motor driving one or two wide fabric belts, and leans away from it while the belt vibrates the target area.
No specific data on Vibro-Slim. Wikipedia reports that by the 1980s it had become clear that belt machines provided no fat-reducing benefit.

angle.text: The category was sold on a slimmer waist without exercise; this was a marketing claim of the period.

lead: Vibro-Slim is described as a 1928 vibration device for weight loss. The following describes the product's category, the vibrating belt machine.

Vibrating belt machines were promoted as passive fat reduction. Gustav Zander devised early versions in the late 1800s for massage, and from 1927 John Harvey Kellogg promoted the Battle Creek Health Builder, with a 1927 Vogue advertisement showing Vivienne Segal using one [1]. Marketers claimed the vibration broke up abdominal fat; later reporting says they gave no fat-reducing benefit [1].

paras: A typical machine had a platform and a waist-high post with an electric motor driving fabric belts [1]. They were most popular in the 1950s and 1960s and became a comic staple of television, including I Love Lucy and The Flintstones [1]. Portable versions have continued to be advertised in infomercials [1].

timeline.event: Kellogg promotes the Battle Creek Health Builder [1]
